hints: Compare the C-Cl bond in chlorobenzene with the C-Cl bond in a chloroalkane like chloroethane. Think about what extra feature the benzene ring provides that an alkane cannot.
Focus on the lone pairs on Cl or O. What orbital are they in, and how could that orbital interact side-on with the pi electron cloud of the ring?
If electrons from X become delocalised into the ring, what happens to the bond order and bond strength of the C-X bond, and how does that affect breaking it?
walkthrough:
Picture what is different about X attached to a ring**
In a chloroalkane the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond is a simple single sigma bond. In chlorobenzene or phenol the $\text{Cl}$ or $\text{O}$ atom sits directly attached to the delocalised pi system. That direct attachment lets something extra happen that never happens in aliphatic compounds.

Spot the overlapping p-orbital**
Both $\text{Cl}$ and $\text{O}$ in $\text{OH}$ have lone pairs in a p-orbital. That p-orbital is in the correct orientation to overlap sideways with the p-orbitals that make up the benzene pi cloud. So the lone pair is not stuck on X, it can interact with the ring.

See the partial double bond form**
Because of that overlap, one lone pair becomes delocalised into the ring pi system. This feeds extra electron density between C and X, so the $\text{C-Cl}$ or $\text{C-O}$ bond is no longer a pure single bond. It gains partial double bond character, it is shorter and stronger, and needs much more energy to break. That is why nucleophilic breaking of the $\text{C-X}$ bond does not occur under normal conditions.

Final answer: The $\text{C-X}$ / $\text{C-Cl}$ / $\text{C-O}$ bond is stronger in chlorobenzene / phenol than in aliphatic analogues.
The p-orbital / lone pair on $\text{Cl}$ / $\text{O}$ overlaps with the pi-electron cloud of the benzene ring.
The lone pair electrons delocalise into the ring, giving the $\text{C-X}$ bond partial double bond character, so it is harder to break.

hints: Recall that the $\text{OH}$ group strongly activates the benzene ring toward electrophilic substitution. Which positions on the ring does it direct to?

With bromine in water phenol gives 2,4,6-tribromophenol, but here bromine is in an inert solvent and the product formula is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{BrOH}$, meaning only one Br has entered. Which two mono-substituted isomers correspond to the activated positions?
walkthrough:
Use the directing power of OH**
The $\text{OH}$ group donates its lone pair into the ring, just as in part (a). That makes the ring much more reactive toward electrophiles and directs incoming groups to the 2, 4 and 6 positions, that is ortho and para to $\text{OH}$.

Limit to mono-substitution**
In aqueous bromine you get the white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol because conditions are so vigorous. Here the solvent is inert and the molecular formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{BrOH}$ tells you only one H has been replaced by one Br. So you draw the two distinct possibilities: $\text{Br}$ next to $\text{OH}$ which is 2-bromophenol (ortho), and $\text{Br}$ opposite $\text{OH}$ which is 4-bromophenol (para).

Final answer: Product 1: 2-bromophenol, benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ at position 1 and $\text{Br}$ at ortho position 2.
Product 2: 4-bromophenol, benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ at position 1 and $\text{Br}$ at para position 4.

hints: Step 1 converts benzene to nitrobenzene. What mixture generates the $\text{NO}_2^+$ electrophile, and what temperature keeps it to mono-nitration?
Step 2 converts $\text{NO}_2$ to $\text{NH}_2$. What metal plus acid reducing mixture is standard for this in Paper 4, and what condition is needed?
Step 4 converts diazonium salt K to phenol. What simple reagent replaces the $\text{N}_2^+$ group by $\text{OH}$ when warmed?
walkthrough:
Nitrate benzene under controlled conditions**
To make nitrobenzene you need the nitronium ion $\text{NO}_2^+$. That comes from concentrated nitric acid plus concentrated sulfuric acid acting as catalyst. Keep the temperature at 50 to 55 $^\circ\text{C}$ so you get mono-nitration and avoid dinitration.

Reduce nitro to amine**
The change $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_2$ to $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$ is a 6-electron reduction. The classic Paper 4 reagent is tin plus concentrated hydrochloric acid with heating, followed by neutralisation to release the free amine. $\text{Fe}$ + $\text{HCl}$ with heat is an alternative in general chemistry, but learn $\text{Sn}$ / conc. $\text{HCl}$ and heat here.

Hydrolyse the diazonium salt**
Step 3 has already made the diazonium salt K at 5 $^\circ\text{C}$. To turn $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+$ into phenol you simply warm it with water. The $\text{N}_2$ leaves as nitrogen gas and $\text{OH}$ from water takes its place.

Final answer: step 1: conc. $\text{HNO}_3$ + conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, 50 to 55 $^\circ\text{C}$
step 2: $\text{Sn}$ + conc. $\text{HCl}$, heat
step 4: $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, warm / heat

hints: Step 3 uses $\text{NaNO}_2$(aq) / $\text{HCl}$(aq) at 5 $^\circ\text{C}$ on phenylamine. What type of salt containing $\text{N}\equiv\text{N}^+$ is formed?
walkthrough:
Recognise diazotisation**
Primary aromatic amines with nitrous acid, made in situ from $\text{NaNO}_2$ + $\text{HCl}$, at 0 to 5 $^\circ\text{C}$ give diazonium salts. So K is benzenediazonium chloride, a benzene ring attached to $\text{-N}^+\equiv\text{N}$ with $\text{Cl}^-$ as counter ion: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{-N}^+\equiv\text{N Cl}^-$.

hints: Benzene to nitrobenzene involves attack of $\text{NO}_2^+$ on the pi ring while aromaticity is restored. What class of benzene mechanism is this?
walkthrough:
Name the nitration mechanism**
Benzene acts as a nucleophile toward the $\text{NO}_2^+$ electrophile, forms a temporary carbocation intermediate, then loses $\text{H}^+$. A hydrogen on the ring is substituted by $\text{NO}_2$, so this is electrophilic substitution.

hints: Step 2 is reduction of $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_2$ to $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$ using [H]. Balance O atoms by adding $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and then balance H atoms with [H]. How many [H] are needed to remove two O atoms as water?
walkthrough:
Balance the reduction with [H]**
Think of [H] as hydrogen that adds electrons plus protons. Nitrobenzene $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_2$ must lose two O atoms and gain two H atoms on N to become $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$. Each O is removed as $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, so you need $2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ on the right. Counting H: right side has $2 + 4 = 6$ H beyond the phenyl group, so you need $6[\text{H}]$ on the left: $$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_2 + 6[\text{H}] \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
